question.text: During the reign of this emperor, the siege of the Masada ended the First Jewish Revolt. This emperor is said to have fiddled during the Great Fire of Rome.
question.clue: This leader's mother Agrippina the Younger was initially his regent, but he eventually had her assassinated.

swap.leadin: This man was the first Roman emperor.
swap.text: Name this adopted son of Julius Caesar and member of the Second Triumvirate.
swap.clue: During his reign, the Pantheon was constructed on the commission of Marcus Agrippa.

question.leadin: The eventual losing side in this conflict was expelled from the Iberian Peninsula with their loss at the Battle of Ilipa.
question.text: Identify this conflict whose notable leaders included Mago and Hasdrubal, the latter of whom led troops in losing efforts at the Battles of Baecula and the Metaurus.
question.clue: The deadliest battle in this war saw Paullus and Varro drawn into a double encirclement and lose 50 000 men.

swap.leadin: To complete this siege, attacking forces built a wall around a hilltop fort, then built a wall around themselves to protect from a reinforcing army.
swap.text: Name this 52 BCE siege of a hilltop fort commanded by Vercingetorix, whose surrender essentially guaranteed the fall of Gaul.
swap.clue: A group of Mandubii civilians became trapped between the two sides of this battle and were left to starve.

question.leadin: A letter to Tacitus that described an eruption of this volcano detailed the death of the admiral of the Misenum fleet.
question.text: Name this mountain near the Bay of Naples, whose AD 79 eruption destroyed the nearby town of Herculaneum.
question.clue: Artifacts excavated from towns next to this feature were confined to a Secret Museum due to their incredibly erotic content.

swap.leadin: Lars Porsena was a king of these peoples who ruled from Clusium.
swap.text: Name these peoples that fought against the Romans in a namesake "League" while attempting to restore Tarquin the Proud to the throne.
swap.clue: One of these people's cities was Veii, and they lived in Tuscany.

question.leadin: This man's wife drove over her dead father's body with a chariot in a road now known as the "Street of Crime."
question.text: Name this man who usurped Servius Tullius to become king of Rome. He himself was popularly overthrown after his son Sextus raped a woman named Lucretia.
question.answerHtml: Tarquin the Proud (or Lucius Tarquinius Superbus; prompt on Lucius Tarquinius)
question.clue: This last king of Rome was legendarily deposed and exiled after his son Sextus raped Lucretia, the wife of Lucius Collatinus.

swap.leadin: Answer some questions about Roman priesthoods.
swap.text: These Roman priestesses took thirty-year vows of chastity. The chief duty of these priestesses was to tend the eternal fire of Rome.
swap.clue: According to Plutarch, these people were punished by being sealed in a chamber near the Colline Gate with only limited food and water.

question.text: Androgynous priests known as Galli facilitated the worship of this Roman cult deity. Priests bathed in bull's blood to honor this mother goddess, whose cult became popular during the Second Punic War.

swap.text: Piux IX installed a statue of this first pope in his namesake basilica in the Vatican. As an apostle this man denied Jesus three times.
swap.clue: This very first pope is the patron saint of bakers and Las Vegas. He's often depicted standing at the gates of heaven allowing people in.

question.leadin: Answer the following about Roman occupation of Britain.
question.text: As governor of Britannia, this Roman general subdued the Caledonians and Ordovices, winning the battle of Mons Graupius in Scotland. Father-in-law of Tacitus, he was recalled by Domitian, but not before he circumnavigated Britain.
question.clue: He served under Salvius Titianus after being appointed quaestor in Asia and after he shared a battle tent with his military tutor Suetonius Paulinus.

swap.leadin: This structure stretched 73 miles from Wallsend-on-Tyne to Solway Firth.
swap.text: Identify this structure that was built by the Romans as a defense mechanism against barbarians in England. Begun in AD 122, its namesake emperor also dealt with the Bar Kokhba revolt in Judea.
swap.clue: A birthday invitation was found on one of the Vindolanda tablets, which were unearthed near this structure.

question.leadin: Viriathus led a rebellion that Polybius called the "fiery war" in this region, where velites ("WAY-lee-tace") units failed to counter weapons like the pilum ("PEE-loom") and falcata in the Numantine War.
question.text: Identify this region that contained the mysterious Tartessos civilization. After Sulla's civil war, Quintus Sertorius led a revolt in this region, where "New Carthage" controlled rich silver mines before the Battle of Ilipa ("ILL-ipp-uh").
question.answerHtml: Hispania [accept Iberia or Iberian peninsula; accept Spain or España; accept Portugal; accept Catalonia or Catalunya; accept Hispania Baetica or Hispania Tarraconensis or Hispania Citerior or Hispania Ulterior; accept Lusitania or Lusitanian War; accept Andalusia or Andalucía; accept Murcia] (“New Carthage” is Cartagena.)
question.clue: Hasdrubal Gisco lost to a "reverse Cannae" at Ilipa ("ILL-ih-puh") in this region, which was later the location of the Numantine War.

swap.text: Roman Senators were marked by having a purple stripe on this popular Roman garment, wrapped around the body, which includes the praetexta variety.
swap.clue: The praetexta variety of these semicircular items included a purple band and were used by magistrates.

question.text: This saint asked, "if Rome can perish, what can be safe?" in a letter written during the invasion. His letters to St. Marcella, who died in Rome during the sack, are the best known sources for her life.

swap.leadin: Suetonius records how a ruler of this region, Ptolemy, was executed by Caligula because his purple cloak drew the attention of the crowd when he entered a theatre.
swap.text: Name this region that, after its annexation by Claudius, was divided into the provinces of Tingitana and Caesariensis. Another king of this region, Bocchus I, betrayed his son-in-law, Jugurtha, to Sulla.
swap.answerHtml: Mauretania [accept Mauretania Tingitana and Mauretania Caesariensis; prompt on North Africa, Maghreb, Algeria, Morocco, or the Atlas Mountains by asking “what was the Roman name of the region?”]
swap.clue: It's not Egypt, but a man named Ptolemy was the last Roman client king of this region; its earlier client kings included the Numidian prince Juba II.

question.leadin: Answer the following about the last stand of paganism in Rome.
question.text: In 384 AD, the orator Quintus Symmachus famously petitioned Valentinian II to restore this great pagan monument in Rome, which had just been removed by Gratian.

swap.text: This villa at Herculaneum contained a trove of texts written by Philodemus. This villa was built by Lucius Calpurnius Piso Caesoninus, the father of Caesar's wife, Calpurnia.
swap.answerHtml: Villa Papyri [or Villa of the Papyri or Villa dei Pisoni]

question.text: Curzio Inghirami botched his staged discoveries of Etruscan "scariths" by using paper instead of this material. The Zagreb Book is an Etruscan text written on this material that was found wrapped around an Egyptian mummy.
question.answerHtml: linen [or flax; accept Liber Linteus, Libri lintei, or linen rolls; prompt on textiles, fabric, or synonyms]

swap.leadin: Identify the following about monumental columns.
swap.text: Mainz was home to a classical column dedicated in honor of Nero to this aspect of the chief god of the Roman state, whose official worship took place at his temple on the Capitoline. The Mainz column was a model for other columns erected to worship this god elsewhere in northern Europe.
